properties.Training: Building Bridges Between Science, Policy And Society: Co-Design Of Solutions For Ocean Sustainability
properties.Description of the training/workshop:
This training will equip participants with the concepts, approaches, tools, and hands-on experience to adopt codesign approaches — bringing together scientists, indigenous knowledge holders, policymakers, community representatives, and other actors to collaboratively develop sustainable solutions to real-life challenges. 
Through expert-led sessions, real-world case studies, peer learning, and a field trip, participants will learn: 
✓ How to overcome common barriers in participatory processes 
✓ Principles of systems thinking, transdisciplinary and co-management and the value of co-design 
✓ How to apply tools and methods for co-design in real-life case studies 
✓ How to facilitate truly inclusive processes 
✓ How to balance power among diverse actors and integrate different knowledge systems 
✓ How to communicate effectively across diverse audiences 
✓ How to build long-term sustainability and societal impact into project plans

properties.Training: The Global Ocean Oxygen Decade (GOOD) and the Ocean Acidification Research for Sustainability (OARS) programmes
properties.Description of the training/workshop: The Summer School provided interdisciplinary training on ocean and atmospheric processes related to ocean deoxygenation and acidification, with a particular focus on tropical marine systems. It engaged graduate students, doctoral candidates, and early-career scientists in the latest methodologies and research on biogeochemical and physical interactions between the ocean and atmosphere and their impacts on marine ecosystems. The programme combined theoretical lectures, laboratory and field-based practical training, and sessions on science communication, ethics in ocean science, stakeholder engagement, and international initiatives including the Ocean Decade.

properties.Training: Enhancing marine biodiversity data collection and publishing
properties.Description of the training/workshop: The workshop focuses on mobilising marine biological observation datasets to the Ocean Biodiversity Information System (OBIS). The objective is to help data holders understand the value of following good practices for standardising biological data, using widely accepted biodiversity standards like Darwin Core. This would include records of different biological attributes and ecosystem observations from different types of sampling methodologies. A complementary activity of the workshop will contemplate a field work day in which participants will receive training on the collection and processing of benthic photo-quadrat imagery and their analysis following MBON Pole to Pole monitoring protocols, aiming to enhance capacity for long-term monitoring of rocky intertidal communities. By the end of the workshop, attendees will have a clear understanding of the process of mobilising biological data to OBIS and will have brought one of their datasets to a final maturity state that aligns with best practices for data sharing and biodiversity documentation.

properties.Training: International Field Training School Taxonomy-based early detection of Alien Invasive Species (AIS) in the Mediterranean marinas
properties.Description of the training/workshop:
The Mediterranean Sea is recognized as one of the world’s hotspots for marine biodiversity. At the same time, it is among the most vulnerable area to biological invasions, which are considered the second greatest threat to marine biodiversity after habitat destruction.
Non-Indigenous Species (NIS), often introduced through ballast water, ship hulls, and other human activities, can cause substantial ecological and economic damage. Early detection is therefore essential to prevent their establishment and spread.
The Barcelona Convention and its SPA/BD Protocol emphasize the protection and conservation of marine and coastal biodiversity. Invasive species threaten biodiversity, ecosystems, and economic sectors such as fisheries, aquaculture, industry, and tourism, as well as human health. Timely detection makes it possible to intervene early, reducing environmental and economic impacts.
Marinas, as hubs of nautical activity and key entry points, are strategic sites for the surveillance of NIS. Establishing a field school in this context provides an opportunity to train regional experts, standardize detection protocols, harmonize surveillance methods, raise awareness among stakeholders, and strengthen both regional cooperation and networking.

properties.Training: Environmental DNA (eDNA) Training for Africa and the Adjacent Island States 2026
properties.Description of the training/workshop:
Environmental DNA (eDNA) sampling and analysis have become an increasingly popular tool for studying biodiversity and monitoring ecosystems. It provides a relatively easy, non-invasive method to scan environments; estimate number of species, assess biodiversity, and monitor changes in a community without having to collect organism samples. Monitoring of endangered species, invasive species, pathogens, and harmful algal bloom Additionally, eDNA has the potential to inform on the movements and habitat associations of endangered/rare species, migratory species, water quality, detecting and tracking invasive species, harmful algal blooms, pathogens, and parasites. eDNA uses traces of genetic materials that organisms leave behind in water, soil, or air. Regardless of its wide application, knowledge of this technique is still underused in several parts of the world, such as in Africa.

Marine ecosystems of Africa and the adjacent island states are teeming with biodiversity, including 439 key marine biodiversity areas. These ecosystems are facing significant threats from climate change, overexploitation, invasive species, urbanization, and other factors, as such, impact on biodiversity. Therefore, there is an urgent need to accelerate the understanding of African biodiversity patterns and monitor ecosystems more efficiently. Implementing eDNA techniques in biodiversity assessment in African countries is a promising opportunity to maximize the conservation and management of marine life. 

In this context, this blended training aims to provide participants with a comprehensive theoretical understanding of environmental DNA (eDNA) and its applications in environmental sciences. It will cover all relevant aspects from eDNA sampling, laboratory and bioinformatic analysis, data analysis of results and possible application. The participants will learn about the origins of eDNA, how it enters the environment, and its significance in measuring biodiversity. The training will give an overview of eDNA, including its definition and different ecosystems where it can be studied with a specific focus on marine ecosystems.

Regardless of its wide application, knowledge of this technique is still underused in several parts of the world, such as in Africa.

Marine ecosystems of Africa and the adjacent island states are teeming with biodiversity, including 439 key marine biodiversity areas. These ecosystems are facing significant threats from climate change, overexploitation, invasive species, urbanization, and other factors, as such, impact on biodiversity. Therefore, there is an urgent need to accelerate the understanding of African biodiversity patterns and monitor ecosystems more efficiently. Implementing eDNA techniques in biodiversity assessment in African countries is a promising opportunity to maximize the conservation and management of marine life. 

In this context, this blended training aims to provide participants with a comprehensive theoretical understanding of environmental DNA (eDNA) and its applications in environmental sciences. It will cover all relevant aspects from eDNA sampling, laboratory and bioinformatic analysis, data analysis of results and possible application. The participants will learn about the origins of eDNA, how it enters the environment, and its significance in measuring biodiversity. The training will give an overview of eDNA, including its definition and different ecosystems where it can be studied with a specific focus on marine ecosystems.

properties.Training: Strengthening Sea Level Monitoring and Data Management in East Africa for Coastal Resilience and Community Safety - Mozambique
properties.Description of the training/workshop: Equipping national data managers, technicians, and research institutions with hands-on skills to handle the full data workflow from sea-level stations - including acquisition, validation, processing, archiving, and dissemination.     Coastal communities in Kenya, Mozambique, Madagascar and the Seychelles face mounting challenges from rising sea levels, yet their capacity to monitor these changes remains limited. Existing observation networks are sparse, with outdated or poorly maintained tide gauges and inconsistent data collection across the region. Many national institutions lack the technical expertise and resources required for data acquisition, quality control, data management, and retrieval, resulting in significant data gaps that undermine coastal planning, early warning systems, and policy development.  The SEAMARCS training directly addresses these gaps by equipping national data managers, technicians, and research institutions with hands-on skills to handle the full data workflow from sea-level stations - including acquisition, validation, processing, archiving, and dissemination. By developing local capacity to manage and share sea-level data efficiently, the training will enhance institutional self-reliance, improve data-driven decision-making, and contribute to more resilient and informed coastal management across the region. To make this project effective in the long term, this training enables local ownership, effective utilization of sea-level data, and retention of technical capacity within national institutions.
